# Transforming Data {#sec-transforming-data}

A project's datasets can be transformed into new datasets.
These transformations are available in the **Transformations** section of the **Data** tab:

- `r keys("Subset")`: Creates a subset of a dataset.
- `r keys("Join")`: Joins two datasets.
- `r keys("Pivot Wider")`: Pivots a dataset wider (i.e., unstacks it).
- `r keys("Pivot Longer")`: Pivots a dataset longer (i.e., stacks it).

The original dataset is not changed.
Instead, the result is added to the project as a new dataset, which can then be used by analyses.

Each of these dialogs includes the following:

**Output name**: Enter the name of the new dataset.
A name is suggested for you, but it must be unique within the project.

**Preview**: Shows the new dataset as it will be created with the current settings.
The preview is limited to the first 300 rows.

## Subset Dataset {#sec-subset-dlg}

This dialog creates a dataset from another dataset that matches a set of filters.

**Dataset**: Select the dataset to subset.

:::: {.optionssection data-latex=""}
::: {.optionssectiontitle data-latex=""}
Filter Type
:::

**Single**: Select this option to filter by a single column.

**AND**: Select this option to filter by multiple columns, where all the filters must match a row for it to be included.

**OR**: Select this option to filter by multiple columns, where a row is included if any of the filters match it.

**Section**: Select this option to include a contiguous block of rows, based on start and end labels in a column.
::::

### Column Filters {-}

These options are available when **Single**, **AND**, or **OR** is selected.

Each filter consists of a column, a comparison operator, and the values to compare against:

- **Column**: The column to compare.
- **Operator**: How to compare the column's values against the provided values.
  The available operators are `=` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `<=` (less than or equal to), `>` (greater than), and `>=` (greater than or equal to).
- **Values**: The values to compare against.
  If multiple values are provided, then a row matches if its value matches any of them.

**Add Filter**: Click this button to add another filter.

**Remove Filter**: Click this button to remove the last filter.

### Section Filter {-}

These options are available when **Section** is selected.
They create a subset which only includes the rows that match the start and end labels and all the rows in between.

**Column**: Select the column to search for the start and end labels.

**Start label**: Select or enter the label that begins the subset.

**End label**: Select or enter the label that marks the end of the subset.

**Include sentinel labels**: Check this option to include the rows with the start and end labels in the subset.
Uncheck it to only include the rows between them.

\newpage

## Join Datasets {#sec-join-dlg}

This dialog combines the columns of two datasets by matching rows on one or more key columns.

**Left dataset**: Select the dataset to join with.

**Right dataset**: Select the dataset being joined with the left one.
All columns except for the key columns will be added to the output.

:::: {.optionssection data-latex=""}
::: {.optionssectiontitle data-latex=""}
Join type
:::

**Left Join (Unique Last)**: All rows and columns from the left dataset are preserved.
If a key in the left dataset matches multiple rows in the right dataset, then only the data from the last matching right row is used.
This is useful for collapsing one-to-many relationships into a single row.

**Left Join (Unique First)**: The same as **Left Join (Unique Last)**, except that only the data from the first matching right row is used.

**Left Join**: A standard left join.
If a key in the left dataset matches multiple rows in the right dataset, then the left row is duplicated for each matching right row.
This means the output may have more rows than the left dataset.
If a left row has no matching right rows, then it is still included, with missing data in the right dataset's columns.

**Inner Join**: Only rows whose keys match in both datasets are included.
If a key in the left dataset matches multiple rows in the right dataset, then the left row is duplicated for each matching right row.
::::

For the left join types, rows in the right dataset whose keys do not appear in the left dataset are ignored.

### Join Columns {-}

Each row in this section is a pair of columns to match on: a **Left Column** from the left dataset and a **Right Column** from the right dataset.
These can be the datasets' ID columns or categorical columns.

**Add Column Pair**: Click this button to add another pair of columns to match on.

**Remove Column Pair**: Click this button to remove the last pair of columns.

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
Categorical labels must match textually between the datasets.
:::

### Options {-}

**Duplicate column suffix**: Enter the text to add to a column from the right dataset if the left dataset already has a column with the same name.
This makes the column's name unique.
The default is *.x*.

\newpage

## Pivot Wider {#sec-pivot-wider-dlg}

Pivoting wider (also known as unstacking, spreading, or casting) creates a single row for each observation.
A categorical column is split into new columns, which are filled with the values from the specified continuous columns.
This is useful for breaking a grouping variable into new columns, so that each row is a unique observation.

**Dataset**: Select the dataset to pivot.

**Select Columns...**: Click this button to open the [**Select Variables**](#sec-select-variables-dlg) dialog and select the following columns:

- **ID columns**: The columns that identify a unique observation.
- **Names from**: The categorical column whose labels will each become a new column.
- **Values from**: The continuous columns whose values will be copied into the new columns.
  If multiple value columns are selected, then a new column is created for each label from every value column.
  If no value columns are selected, then the frequency counts of each unique combination of ID labels are used as the values.

### Options {-}

**Names separator**: If multiple value columns are selected, then enter the separator that joins each label and value column's name.
The default is *\_*.

**Names prefix**: Enter text to prepend to the newly created columns' names.

**Fill value**: If an observation is missing a label that other observations have, then an empty cell is added for that column.
Enter the value to fill these cells with.
The default is missing data (i.e., *NaN*).

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
If multiple rows share the same ID and the same label, then their values are summed together.
:::

\newpage

## Pivot Longer {#sec-pivot-longer-dlg}

Pivoting longer (also known as stacking, gathering, or melting) combines multiple columns into a grouping column and a value column.
This is useful for converting a dataset with one row for each observation into a dataset with grouping columns.

**Dataset**: Select the dataset to pivot.

**Select Columns...**: Click this button to open the [**Select Variables**](#sec-select-variables-dlg) dialog and select the following columns:

- **Columns to keep**: The columns that are not pivoted.
  These are copied to the new dataset, and their values are filled in for all the new rows created from their observation.
  (These are usually the ID and grouping columns.)
  The output is sorted by these columns.
- **Columns to pivot**: The continuous columns to pivot into the longer format.

### Target Columns {-}

**Names to**: Enter the name of the new grouping column, which will use the original columns' names as its groups.
To create multiple grouping columns (see **Names pattern**), enter their names separated by commas.
The default is *variable*.

**Values to**: Enter the name of the new column that the values are moved into.
This column will contain the values from the pivoted columns, stacked on top of each other.
The default is *value*.

**Names pattern**: To split the pivoted columns' names into multiple grouping columns, enter a regular expression here.
It should contain capture groups, where each group will become the value of a new grouping column.
Leave this blank to use the full names of the pivoted columns as the labels.

For example, if the columns to pivot are *math_2023* and *reading_2024*, then a pattern of `(.*)_(.*)` with **Names to** set to *subject, year* would create a *subject* column and a *year* column.
